newsitem.title: SUDAN: Sudan arrests politicians after towns fall.
newsitem.headline: Sudan arrests politicians after towns fall.

text.p: Sudan has arrested up to 15 opposition party members after rebels in the south of the country seized control of two towns on the Ethiopian border, Sudanese parliament speaker Hassan al-Turabi said on Wednesday.

He told Reuters in an interview that the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) and Umma Party members were arrested to maintain order after the border towns of Kurmuk and Qeissan fell to rebels who are fighting the Sudanese government.
There was no immediate confirmation from the Cairo offices of the opposition groups.

Turabi, who is generally seen as the real brain behind Sudan's government and its conversion to a radical Islamist state, said the group was likely to be released in the event the territory is regained.
Asked whether the opposition members had been arrested, Turabi said: "Yes, after this takeover of the frontier towns."

It was not immediately clear how senior the detainees were but a Sudanese official said Sid Ahmed Hussein, the deputy secretary general of the DUP and its senior man inside Sudan, was among the group.
"I think there are about 10 to 15 (in all) from both parties because both of them fully supported what's happening," Turabi said.
"(Umma Party leader) Sadeq al-Mahdi and (DUP's) Mohammed Osman...said 'We are there behind it' and we in Khartoum don't want this to create more disorder," Turabi said.
Mahdi was the democratically elected prime minister in Sudan when the present government seized power in a coup in 1989.
"Sadeq may be tried and the leaders may be tried. These people probably will be detained for a while. Once we restore our territory, probably they will be released," Turabi said.
Mahdi fled Sudan in December and called for the overthrow by popular uprising of the Islamist government.
The previous governments of 1964 and 1985, that were not democratically elected, both fell to uprisings.

"The opposition circulated paper first that they are supporting this war...and immediately when these towns were taken over these people distributed their leaflets so they were arrested. They can be tried of course as someone who allies with an enemy in the criminal law, in any country," Turabi said.
He said the opposition members were held under a public security law but did not know whether any trial had been set.
He alleged that both the United States and Britain were supporting the military activity in the south and east because they too wanted the downfall of the Islamist government.

"It's the United States that's involved in this...they are saying...this is an Islamic country therefore terrorist. Of course the British are also behind it...but they orchestrate their strategy without declaring it," Turabi said.
Sudan has also charged Eritrea and Ethiopia with fighting with the rebels. Both countries deny that they have taken part.
Mahdi has played down the military aspect of the opposition's strategy, saying it was one form of pressure he hoped would tip the balance against the government.
Opposition rebels led by the Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA) have been fighting the Khartoum government since 1983.
A Western diplomat said that this offensive which began earlier this month had scared the government but that the rebels had now lost their momentum.
"They (the opposition) were expecting something more from Kurmuk and Qeissan but I think nothing will happen because it's too late. The momentum is not there," he added.
